items.summary: A European Commission proposal published on Oct. 27, part of a wider reform of the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (the EU border agency), would give Frontex a role in identifying and reporting illegal online content by establishing an Online Monitoring and Response Center within it. The center is intended to counter smuggling networks that use social media to coordinate unauthorized border crossings; it would monitor publicly available social media, notify platforms of illegal material, and seek designation as a trusted flagger under the Digital Services Act (DSA). Under Article 22 of the DSA, platforms must give notices from trusted flaggers priority and process them without undue delay, but that status does not empower an entity to order content removal—platforms remain responsible for assessing notices and deciding how to act. As of Nov. 6, national coordinators had designated 90 trusted flaggers across 22 member states; these include child protection hotlines, anti-discrimination groups, fact-checkers, consumer organizations, copyright holders, private anti-piracy firms, and a handful of public bodies such as financial supervisors in Austria, Belgium, Ireland and Portugal that flag scams and fraud. None is an EU agency or law enforcement body. The Commission says its proposal respects this distinction by separating Frontex's role in identifying and reporting content from platforms assessing notices and national authorities issuing legally binding orders; the proposal would also let Frontex ask national authorities to issue removal orders under Article 9 or request information about individual users under Article 10. A coalition of 28 rights organizations across Europe is calling on the Commission to withdraw the proposed powers, arguing they risk undermining DSA safeguards against government overreach. The dispute sharpens because the proposal comes as the Commission develops guidance on how the trusted flagger system should operate; in May it published draft guidelines consulted until July 10, with final adoption planned for the second half of 2026. Paragraph 31 of those guidelines recommends no overlap between trusted flaggers and public authorities empowered to issue orders against illegal content under Article 9, calling on national Digital Services Coordinators (DSCs) to ensure such powers are not commingled with trusted flagger status—illustrated by a good-practice example in which a coordinator refuses trusted flagger status to a market surveillance authority that can issue removal orders. Civil society argues Frontex's arrangement risks exactly this conflict, writing in a letter to Commissioners Henna Virkkunen and Magnus Brunner published this week that the commingled role would 'logically and inevitably result in its notices to the platforms being treated as proxy takedown orders.' Asha Allen of the Centre for Democracy and Technology Europe (CDT Europe) said the DSA does not provide explicit safeguards against government overreach through trusted flaggers, noting point 31 expressly recommends that authorities who can issue Article 9 and 10 orders should not commingle their role by also being trusted flaggers—so she argued 'this proposal therefore goes against the Commission's own draft guidelines.' She added that although these are detailed and reflect many civil society recommendations, they are not binding rules yet to be adopted. The scope of Frontex's proposed monitoring raises further concerns: it would cover publicly accessible user-generated content relevant to managing external borders and migration, including unauthorized border crossings, migrant smuggling, cross-border crime, violence at borders, disruption of border infrastructure, disinformation, the instrumentalization of migration, and other hybrid threats; it would allow cooperation with non-EU authorities on responding to identified content and require a DSA crisis protocol for situations at external borders. Virkkunen argued criminal smuggling networks are 'growing increasingly professional, adapting rapidly and utilizing new technologies and social media,' that Frontex has the specialist expertise needed for trusted flagger designation (which it would apply for through a national DSC), and that platforms should prioritize notifications—stating if Frontex flags content that is 'clearly disinformation,' online platforms 'should prioritize that.' But Allen noted Article 22 concerns notices about illegal content, not misleading information in general; the DSA does not itself define illegal content (determined by applicable EU and national law), and false or politically sensitive information is not automatically illegal. Civil society argues the monitoring categories are too broadly defined and could capture lawful expression—particularly concerning for migrant and asylum-seeking communities that rely on social media to share border-crossing, route, and support information—and points to a history of law enforcement using national security arguments to pressure companies into removing content with disproportionate consequences for marginalized groups. Allen cited a 2022 case in which the Oversight Board established by Meta overturned removal of a UK drill music clip from Instagram following a request from London's Metropolitan Police, calling Meta's channels for government requests 'haphazard and opaque.' The Commission maintains that its Oct. 27 remarks show 'the DSA enforcement framework remains fully respected,' with Frontex able to act within its mandate on detection and signaling while engaging platforms directly; the proposal must still be negotiated by the European Parliament and Council, no adoption timeline has been announced, and even if adopted Frontex would need designation by a national DSC—most likely in Poland where it is headquartered. The Commission did not respond to a request for comment.
items.title: Frontex Proposal Tests DSA Trusted Flagger Safeguards Amid Civil Society Pushback

Singapore-listed shipbuilder Penguin International has disputed a United Nations panel's conclusion that its sale of two vessels ultimately shipped to Libya violated an arms embargo. In a bourse filing on Nov 17, the company said the transaction involved a security vessel and a landing craft sold in December 2024 to Dubai-based 2020 Volume Boats. Both vessels were delivered from Penguin's yard in Singapore before being shipped to Benghazi, Libya.

On Mar 24, 2026, the UN Panel of Experts on Libya published a report naming Penguin and its wholly owned subsidiary, Penguin Shipyard Asia. The panel classified the security vessel as a naval-type fast patrol vessel and the landing craft as a dual-use vessel, considering their transfer to Libya a violation of an arms embargo imposed under UN Security Council Resolution 1970. However, the panel did not recommend sanctions against Penguin or its subsidiary.

Penguin said it disagreed with the panel's characterisation of the vessels and its conclusion that the transaction breached the embargo. The company maintained both were designed and built for commercial purposes and delivered without arms or ammunition on board. It noted corresponding with the UN panel between January and May in 2025, providing requested information about the transaction.

Penguin said it became aware of the report in September 2026, roughly six months after publication, then engaged Singapore legal counsel and an international sanctions specialist to assess implications. Based on that advice, being named in the report did not itself constitute a sanctions action or impose direct penalties, and the likelihood of UN sanctions against Penguin or its subsidiary was low.

Separately, Penguin has been corresponding with Singapore Customs since November 2025 regarding the export of the vessels. The company said the matter had not materially disrupted operations, and its board was not presently aware of any material financial impact.
items.title: Penguin International disputes UN Libya arms-embargo finding

The author, running locally on a Windows PC called Orthrus (two RTX 4090s) and an M5 MacBook with 32 GB of unified memory, wanted to run larger models without relying on online services. Strata was recommended for MoE inference: only the hot experts stay in VRAM while the rest go to RAM or disk, letting a ~180B model fit on consumer hardware like an RTX 4090. On the laptop, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ran at 13.5 tok/s via Strata—too slow for coding-agent use but worth exploring, since many MoE models exceed a MacBook's unified memory.

Before committing to Strata, the author examined how llama.cpp, vLLM, and Transformers handle offloading when experts don't fit. llama.cpp maps GGUF files with mmap; only activations cross PCIe while weights stay on CPU, but page-cache thrashing occurs when they don't fit, and a new GPU expert cache fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) losing ~10% even when everything fits. vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N pins weights in RAM read over PCIe; for MoE only routed experts are offloaded with no caching, so hot experts cross PCIe every token and there is no disk tier—fine for large batches but not one user on one GPU. Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), copying a whole layer's expert bank to the GPU per module; it has no cache or routing awareness, and on a Mac CPU/GPU shared memory means "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

Benchmarks ran Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB) with ample RAM: offloading only experts doubled vLLM's speed, FP8 helped further by halving bytes per expert and fitting more of the model on GPU, while vLLM's pre-copied-layer backend ran under 1 tok/s. When experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat; when they don't, one must stream only what the router picks through a bounded cache fast enough that SSD—not Python—is the bottleneck.

The author built an expert-streaming path directly into Transformers (PR huggingface/transformers#50717), with all code generated by AI and their role limited to choosing experiments, reading profiles, and deciding what to keep. Starting on OLMoE-1B-7B (which fits in memory) for per-token comparison: the first version cached experts on disk with an LRU cache and a Python loop running one expert at a time—10.1 tok/s versus ~32 vanilla—the bottleneck being their loop, not I/O. The key fix turned the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers plus a per-layer table mapping expert id to slot; remapping router ids made grouped_mm run on it unchanged (no custom matmul), reaching 34.6 tok/s versus 38.1 vanilla.

Moving to Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, the model has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active) totaling 121 GB in FP8, plus a separate 51 GB n-gram embedding table needing its own disk path: experts quantized to 3 bits occupy ~49 GB on disk with 12 GiB cached; dense layers run at 8 bits (~5.4 GB, +0.2% perplexity vs BF16); the n-gram table stays on disk read per row. Conversion takes ~5 hours; after loading it uses ~18 GiB and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB—near the limit before macOS swapping.

On the same M5 with identical prompts, Strata (0.1.60) used IQ3_XXS experts while both ran greedy with thinking, MTP, and speculative drafts off and 1,024-token prefill chunks; vllm-metal streams routed experts from an MLX checkpoint but cannot run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB because only experts stream and n-gram tables stay in memory (~5 GB of dense layers plus any expert cache). Most time was spent outside the experts: committing GPU work early after each block gave +10% (PyTorch holds small kernels until sync); Metal kernels handled Gated DeltaNet and hyper-connections lacking fast macOS paths; switching to Strata's GGUF weights cut dense weight traffic from 5.4 GB to 3.9 GB per token and expert size from 2.15 MB to 1.75 MB with separate cache pools; prefill rose from 68 to ~228 tok/s using bigger chunks and reading the next layer's experts while computing the current one; long documents used attention over indexer-selected blocks plus a KV cache that grows in place instead of copying each token; misses were handled by reading just one guessed expert per layer rather than leaving SSD idle. Final results came within ~6% behind Strata on short decode with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

The remaining gap is mostly host round trips (~10 ms per token); waking after a sync accounts for only ~1 ms—the rest is the GPU idling while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues a whole token's work up front and waits on a Metal shared event at each layer, which PyTorch doesn't expose; a flag-spinning hack produced unreliable results (a second to never), so no native MPS op was built due to hang risk.

The author concludes Transformers didn't beat Strata and closing the last ~6% requires deeper stack changes starting with per-layer sync control. The approach's value lies in how closely it got there: streaming only routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on unchanged, and targeted Metal kernels—no C++ extension, just Python, runtime-compiled Metal via torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt Hub kernels.

The generic implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717 with benchmarks in the Space; feedback is welcome. Thanks are given to Pedro, Lysandre, Arthur for feedback, Harry for testing vLLM, and Niko Veit (Strata), whose numbers set the bar that pushed this work forward.
items.title: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers: Streaming Experts Directly from SSD

items.summary: Earlier this year, Google introduced Project Genie as an experimental research prototype for generating and exploring interactive worlds. Today it is rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, who can also join the waitlist on the same page; Google AI Pro members may access via that waitlist. The update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent for building worlds from natural-language conversation, and a community gallery for discovering, exploring, and remixing worlds. Project Genie combines Google's most advanced world models with Gemini models so users can generate, enter, and shape worlds directly in their browser. Genie 4 is described as the company's most realistic and interactive world model yet; it lets users prompt mid-session to change a created world—shifting weather, adding characters, or redirecting action—in real time while navigating. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as scenes unfold, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie's model picker for longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces; today's updates include extended sessions and world chaining (up to 3 minutes per generation, up from 60 seconds, or linking multiple worlds together), 360-degree panorama image grounding to seed new worlds, and real-time in-world events triggered by natural-language prompts. The Project Genie agent lets users describe a vision in natural language while the agent orchestrates Google's multimodal models to craft initial visuals establishing the world's signature look alongside custom background scores tailored to the mood; Gemini can also be brought into sessions to observe on-screen activity, surface context-aware suggestion chips for where to go next, or trigger in-world events automatically. The new gallery combines curated worlds with community creations: 'Living Memory' transforms personal photos into explorable spaces, 'Dino Field Guide' features prehistoric habitats grounded in 360-degree panoramas, and 'Rock Paper Scissors' pits themed objects against one another on a desk with Gemini as real-time referee. Collaborations include creative technologist Will aka BLVCKL!GHT's gothic manor mystery 'Villa Giallo,' and filmmaker Anand Gandhi's ant-colony experience 'The Life of Ants.' Users can launch new worlds from prompts, remix existing gallery experiences by tweaking world structure, soundtrack, or rules with the agent, and publish creations to the community gallery. On safety, all generated video and audio includes SynthID watermarking, and all model inputs and outputs undergo safety screenings; Genie 3 and Genie 4 remain frontier research models as Google works on challenges including camera latency, physical interactions, real-time audio precision, and long-term scene permanence.
items.title: Google rolls out Genie 4 and expanded Project Genie to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers

items.summary: A bipartisan pair of US senators wrote a letter on Tuesday urging Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and White House AI czar, to identify and fix vulnerabilities in US infrastructure following nationwide outages at major companies and government agencies. Maria Cantwell, top Democrat on the Senate commerce, science, and transportation committee, joined Mike Rounds, Republican chair of the Senate subcommittee on cybersecurity, in sending the letter. They cited concerns sparked by reports of AI accessing major banks, cyber-attacks in Japan, and other disruptions. In their writing they stated: 'The fundamental problem is that AI can discover software weaknesses and help attackers exploit them faster than many organizations can respond.' The senators also warned that even when fixes are available, testing and installing patches across interconnected systems can take weeks or months, potentially disrupting essential services. Over the preceding week, tech outages at major banks, workplace communication systems, and federal infrastructure including the Federal Aviation Administration triggered a four-hour nationwide flight stoppage that grounded or delayed thousands of flights, raising alarms about potential cyber-attacks. Top officials maintained the disruptions stemmed from software patch updates intended to address AI harms rather than malicious activity. Clayton testified before the House homeland security committee on Wednesday, telling lawmakers: 'Based on what we know today, after a great deal of diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.' Homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin and deputy FBI director Christopher Raia similarly said they had no reason to believe the outages were connected or the result of an attack. Clayton told CNBC on Tuesday that many organizations are patching legacy systems known for vulnerabilities, noting: 'It is time for an upgrade across our digital infrastructure.' Senate intelligence committee chair Mark Warner echoed this view on X, writing that AI enables identification of vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating pressure to patch immediately and putting strain on systems not built to handle such pace. Secretary of State Marco Rubio attempted to quell speculation by assuring Americans the outages were not linked or tied to malicious actors. JD Vance canceled his scheduled interview at the New York Times' DealBook summit on Wednesday, citing need to attend meetings about the tech outages. Cantwell and Rounds requested that Clayton provide cybersecurity tools to critical infrastructure including hospitals, utilities, small government, and federal agencies, and asked that US teams secure AI systems deployed to find software vulnerabilities against unauthorized access. The senators acknowledged uncertainty: it remains unclear what exactly caused the widespread outages or whether AI played a role.
items.title: US senators urge White House AI chief to fix vulnerabilities after mass outages

Tesla is rolling out stricter driver monitoring for its Full Self-Driving (FSD) system in Europe, while simultaneously loosening supervision requirements in the United States. In Europe, on November 16, the Dutch vehicle authority RDW approved a new update to Tesla Assisted Driving—the name Tesla now uses for FSD (Supervised)—covering HW4 vehicles and delivered over the air. Under this update, drivers receive attention warnings earlier; if they are not paying attention during a manoeuvre, they receive a full strike. There is also a speed component: above 130 km/h (81 mph), where legal, the driver must keep their hands on the wheel. Additionally, setting a maximum speed above what the system displays now requires confirmation by scrolling the wheel up, with the speed limit sign pulsing red when the car exceeds it. The RDW tested the update on its own track and public roads, reporting no adverse or unintended effects; ten other countries have adopted the Dutch approval so far—Finland is among them—with EU-wide approval still pending a vote at the TCMV, the committee of member states. This follows two weeks earlier when Tesla cut the system's speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in Europe and dropped the 'Full Self-Driving' name there; Germany had made both changes a condition of supporting EU approval.

In contrast, Tesla has spent much of the past year loosening supervision domestically. At its shareholder meeting last November, Musk complained that the car was 'a little strict about keeping your eyes on the road,' saying Tesla would allow texting within a month or two; when an owner asked whether FSD v14.2.1 allowed texting, Musk replied it depended on surrounding traffic context. In May, Musk confirmed FSD v14.3.3 was built to nag drivers less—though Tesla did add better eye-gaze tracking and eyewear handling in a June build—the pitch of fewer nags remains sold as a feature. US drivers have been permitted hands-free operation at any speed since Tesla moved to cabin-camera monitoring in 2024, with no equivalent 130 km/h rule.

NHTSA has taken notice: in its engineering analysis of FSD crashes in low-visibility conditions, the agency asked Tesla to justify a list of marketing claims and specifically cited Musk's texting post. In September, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi directed NHTSA to investigate Tesla's driver monitoring after numerous videos appeared to show drivers asleep on Autopilot and FSD. Recent incidents include a driver who told CHP he was asleep while his Tesla drove through a freeway closure and struck a patrol car, seriously injuring two officers; owners are also filming themselves defeating the system for online attention.

Both markets receive identical cabin cameras and HW4 computers. The divergence stems from regulatory structure: in Europe, a type-approval authority tests every update before shipment and can refuse it, whereas in the US no one pre-approves driver-assist software—Tesla self-certifies and NHTSA intervenes only after complaints and crashes accumulate.

Electrek's Take argues this proves Tesla can build stricter monitoring whenever demanded—the code already runs on HW4 cars across 11 European countries. The article contends that if FSD were truly safe enough to relax supervision, Tesla would be presenting RDW data proving looser monitoring is safe rather than adding warnings and harsher strikes; instead it does the opposite in Europe because required, and the opposite in the US because permitted. Electrek asserts FSD becomes more dangerous as it improves—because people trust it more and watch less—and that the answer requires monitoring to tighten as the system improves, which Europe is enforcing while the US loosens it, encourages illegal phone use from leadership, and leaves drivers with 100% of liability when things go wrong. The piece closes by questioning why European owners receive earlier warnings and instant strikes but American owners do not on identical software—or whether NHTSA will be forced to act.

Note: An unrelated EnergySage advertisement appears in the source text promoting home solar, lease/PPA options, 10% electricity rate increases last year, and savings of 20–30%; it is excluded from this summary.
items.title: Tesla Applies Stricter FSD Driver Monitoring in Europe While Loosening It in the US

items.summary: West Coast Customs (WCC) has completed Project B-Zero, its first all-electric Chevrolet Bel Air. The Burbank shop cut the body off a Tesla Model 3 and mounted a 1955 Bel Air shell over it while keeping the entire rolling platform intact; the result charges at Tesla Superchargers. Founder and CEO Ryan Friedlinghaus said longtime client Troy Swope, who is converting his whole car collection to electric, chose the Bel Air as its first project after WCC had previously built him a gas-powered Chevelle. Rather than extract the Model 3's motors and battery to fit them into the old Chevy, Friedlinghaus kept the Tesla whole with the Chevy serving only as a body kit, describing it as his shop's signature 'old school meets new school' formula that he has applied for years using other cars of the same model on updated chassis. The build was tedious but drove fine even when tested bare without doors, lights or seatbelts. The main engineering challenge was wheelbase: a 1955 Chevy rides at 115 inches versus the Model 3's 113.2 inches, and because the Tesla floor is its battery pack it cannot be cut like gas builds allow. WCC solved this by stretching the Bel Air's rear wheel wells so the wheels sit where they appear to belong. Externally, the car reads as a mostly stock red Bel Air with a satin finish and gloss black accents; internally it retains the Tesla Model 3 interior, including its steering wheel and center touchscreen modified for the Chevy body, plus black suede seats with white octagon stitching that Friedlinghaus said was borrowed from the Lamborghini Urus, along with red accents and 'B-Zero' script on the dash. Friedlinghaus's stated goal is a car that looks like a nice Bel Air outside but reveals itself as a Tesla when opened or pulled into a Supercharger station. Reactions have been split: some are upset about electrifying a Bel Air while others praise it, with client Swope in the latter camp and describing the build as easy to drive and every trip an event. Electrek noted that this approach preserves Tesla's crash structure, battery thermal management, software, over-the-air updates and Supercharger access by never disassembling the car, making it closer to what S-Klub did with its Model 3-based Mercedes 300SL than a traditional drivetrain swap; for comparison, an earlier Sacramento project converting a 1966 Mustang took about $40,000 and two years. The article closes with an unrelated advertisement promoting home solar through EnergySage.
items.title: West Coast Customs builds an electric 1955 Chevy Bel Air on a Tesla Model 3 platform

items.summary: Democratic lawmakers on three congressional committees have demanded documents and records from Howard Lutnick, the US commerce secretary, regarding his handling of Nvidia while his family firm held a large stake in the company. According to Democrats, Cantor Fitzgerald—the investment firm Lutnick ran for decades before joining the Trump administration—held shares in Nvidia worth 'hundreds of millions of dollars' as he made key decisions affecting the tech firm's ability to operate. Lawmakers Jamie Raskin of Maryland, Gregory Meeks of New York, and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California asked whether Lutnick compromised US national security interests to benefit his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald. In a letter on Tuesday addressed to Brandon Lutnick, who now chairs Cantor Fitzgerald, the trio requested communications concerning Nvidia and sought to determine whether decisions about export controls, enforcement measures, or national security policies were improperly influenced by Cantor Fitzgerald's holdings. They also asked whether Lutnick blocked efforts to stop suspected smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China while his family firm held hundreds of millions in stock. In an accompanying news release, the lawmakers cited a New York Times report that Lutnick pushed to weaken rules affecting south-east Asian datacenters, some of which are Cantor Fitzgerald clients. The letter states that at the time of Lutnick's confirmation as commerce secretary in February 2025—when he transferred his stake in Cantor Fitzgerald to trusts benefiting his adult children—the firm had 'amassed a significant stake' in Nvidia, reportedly holding more than 3.5m shares valued at over $1.3bn. In response, a Cantor Fitzgerald spokesperson told the Guardian that these claims were inaccurate and described Cantor's Nvidia holdings as arising primarily from equity swaps executed for clients rather than a proprietary position; the decline since early 2025 reflects unwinding of those hedges as clients closed or reduced swap positions. The firm denied any role in US export control or entity list decisions, called allegations that its work influenced government decisions baseless, and expressed confidence it operated ethically and in compliance with all rules. A commerce department spokesperson told the Times that Lutnick makes policy based on the best interests of the US and does not discuss department matters with his sons, nor do his sons discuss Cantor Fitzgerald business with him. The lawmakers asked Cantor Fitzgerald for written confirmation by 5pm ET on 1 December that it had implemented appropriate preservation measures to retain potentially responsive records. These demands follow Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia last week amid reports of multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, suspected of being a Chinese spy; both Huang and Lutnick are scheduled to testify before Congress next month. The developments also place Lutnick in focus after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the commerce department for not imposing export restrictions on certain Nvidia chips to China.
items.title: Democrats demand answers from Commerce Secretary Lutnick over Nvidia and Cantor Fitzgerald stake

On November 18, 2026, Federal Reserve Bank of New York President Michael S. Barr spoke at the conference 'Making Missing Markets: Catalyzing Capital and Igniting Innovation,' hosted by the New York Fed in New York City. He chose New York as the venue for two reasons: it is the center of American finance, making it a fitting place to discuss incentivizing private investment, and the city has successfully attracted investment into lower-income neighborhoods over recent decades—reversing forces that once linked parts of the city with urban decline. Barr recalled seeing this progress firsthand 30 years ago touring the South Bronx with Treasury Secretary Bob Rubin, where public–private partnerships were building housing, creating businesses and jobs, and making streets safer block by block.

Barr then turned to the economic backdrop for community investment—how fast the economy grows, how well it creates jobs, and how incomes keep up with living costs. He described the overall economy as strong, with low unemployment, solid consumer spending, and robust business investment, but noted that inflation is too high and making it hard for American families to make ends meet. Because of this, he said it is important for the Fed to bring inflation back down to its 2% target in a timely way, adding that if the economy evolves as currently forecast, raising rates further would be appropriate on behalf of Americans; he noted he will continue monitoring incoming data and evolving forecasts.

Barr argued that strong and sustainable communities are key to American prosperity: when resilient, people see a future there and invest—buying homes, shopping locally, starting businesses—and can weather hard times because they believe jobs and opportunities will return. He stressed the Fed's commitment to building stronger communities while acknowledging that not all families and communities are thriving; wealthier households do well, but middle- and lower-income households struggle as the economy leaves some communities behind. Recent estimates put 44% of Americans in low-income communities where a fifth or more live below the poverty line, and these areas often lack sufficient investment in housing, business, and infrastructure.

The Fed's recent Survey of Consumer Finances confirms that most households have very little wealth, and lower-wealth households are nearly four times as likely to say they cannot rely on friends and family for financial help or provide it themselves. Barr asked how this inability to give or receive help reverberates across a community—when jobs lag, ties connecting families and neighbors erode—and noted that despite a strong economy, some people struggle to find good-paying work.

On what investments drive lasting opportunity, Barr emphasized successful public–private partnerships requiring the public sector at all government levels, the private sector, and the nonprofit sector. He explained that market failures often prevent private investment on its own—for example, information asymmetries make it hard for commercial banks to see opportunities in low-income areas—but when banks partner with local, state, and national community development groups including Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs), those partnerships help extend credit, investment, and services to those who need them most while assisting banks in reaching new customers. These organizations reduce the costs of acquiring and interpreting information about borrowers and communities, coordinate lending to overcome collective action problems, and share risks to reduce bank exposures.

Barr said targeting investments at root causes helps capital find successful strategies early, establishing funding infrastructure that sets community-focused projects on a course for long-term investment—echoing what President John Williams said in inaugurating this conference in 2024: it is about investing in solutions leading to long-term partnerships and sustainable success. He noted that addressing root causes means also considering the longer-term outlook for communities, with investments focusing on jobs, housing, schools, infrastructure, and similar areas being critical.

To illustrate, Barr cited several regional examples. In a part of Brooklyn marked by limited housing plus a lack of employment and healthy food sources, partners built City Point, which includes a full-service supermarket, 120 affordable housing units, and retail space for local small businesses—showing how the New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) can leverage private investment into communities. Barr said he helped launch the bipartisan NMTC about a quarter century ago and is pleased it was recently made permanent by Congress. In Middletown, New York, the city converts a long-vacant historic railway station into a community center with a Head Start program in an area where childcare options are sparse, financed partly by the NMTC.

In Syracuse, New York, announced earlier this year is a revolving loan fund for mixed-income housing that provided $30 million in seed money, with private partners contributing the remaining $120 million. Barr noted the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) has been critical to community recovery—helping create or preserve nearly 4 million units of housing over the past 40 years—and pointed out that the Bronx lost roughly a fifth of its housing between 1970 and 1980, along with about a fifth of its population. With help from the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), LIHTC, CDFIs, and other factors, it recovered that ground and continues to recover.

Barr said all these projects are underpinned by the CRA, which has increased lending, investment, and services in low-income communities nationwide. Critical to its success are banks of all sizes—biggest national-market banks, regional banks, specialized-model banks, and community banks—in urban, suburban, small-town, and rural settings. These banks often partner with CDFIs, civil rights groups, chambers of commerce, and others; CDFIs serve as 'boots on the ground' financial providers connecting stakeholders across sectors, and grants to these groups can make the difference between success and failure for banks trying to help communities—in rural areas, small towns, big cities, and Native American lands alike.

Barr noted he has spoken mostly about community development in New York since they are in the Second District, but has seen similar work firsthand across Reserve Bank Districts. He described listening to bankers, CDFIs, and local entrepreneurs come together in Clarksdale, Mississippi; seeing affordable housing built by partnerships between tribal governments and local banks on the Flathead and Blackfeet Reservations in Montana; Working Cities in East Hartford, Connecticut; community-based learning in Portland, Oregon; the transformation and entrepreneurial spirit of Detroit, Michigan; public–private partnership gains for employment and small business growth in Cleveland, Ohio; a business incubator making a difference in Atlanta, Georgia; entrepreneurs in Mesa and Tempe, Arizona who highlighted local community development corporations' role; Chicago educational leaders stressing linking with local employers to chart job pathways for young people from disadvantaged backgrounds; and CDFIs' importance as told by leaders in Kansas City, Missouri, Omaha, Nebraska.

Barr concluded that this good work is happening across the country—in urban, rural, and tribal communities, and in every Reserve Bank District—and framed why they are gathered at the New York Fed. He noted that one part of the building's staff works daily to implement monetary policy, ensure smooth financial markets, and promote a strong economy, but stressed that a strong economy cannot be achieved without strong communities. Core to the Fed's mission, he said, is the Federal Reserve System's Community Development function; he applauded the New York Fed for bringing attention to the untapped potential of low- and moderate-income communities across the United States and noted there is much more they can do together.

The speech carries a disclaimer that views are Barr's own and not necessarily those of his colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee. The document includes nine footnotes citing sources, including Brookings (April 16, 2025), FEDS Notes from the Board of Governors (October 9, 2026), Barr's own March 24, 2026 National Community Investment Conference speech in Phoenix, John C. Williams's November 14, 2024 New York City conference speech, HUD data on LIHTC, and Metropolitics plus the Office of the New York State Comptroller.
items.title: Barr on Investing in America's Underserved Communities at New York Fed Conference

On Wednesday (Nov 18), global equities fell in choppy trading after Nvidia's quarterly report, ahead of Anthropic's market debut. The US dollar strengthened to a fresh 19-month high following comments from Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller on CNBC; he said the central bank needs either to approve a half-point rate hike at its December meeting or signal a faster pace of hikes in 2027. Juan Perez, senior director of trading at Monex USA in Washington, noted that the Fed appears determined to raise rates and possibly do so aggressively, which is carrying the dollar.

Mining stocks dragged European shares lower, while Nvidia's results initially helped Asian markets with Korea's Kospi up 2 per cent overnight; however, the rally fizzled as Nvidia fell 2.4 per cent after rising as much as 2.7 per cent. Nvidia's board dismissed rehiring former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week, though the company forecast sales ahead of Wall Street targets.

Jay Peters, portfolio manager at NewEdge Wealth, said: "The central question Nvidia faces is not related to this earnings report ... it's more about what the company may look like in 3-5 years without a visionary leader like Jensen and as competition from other chipmakers takes shape." The next health check on the AI industry will come with Anthropic preparing to price its shares Wednesday ahead of its debut.

In US markets, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.84 per cent to 50,334.82, the S&P 500 eased 0.07 per cent to 7,335.43, and the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.46 per cent to 24,439.22. MSCI's global gauge fell 0.34 per cent to 1,075.82; the pan-European STOXX 600 dropped 1.03 per cent; emerging market stocks eased 0.13 per cent while Japan's Nikkei rose 0.28 per cent.

In currencies, the dollar index rose 0.19 per cent to 103.81 with the euro down 0.24 per cent at $1.0971. In commodities, crude fell after US inventories rose more than expected: US crude dropped 4.39 per cent to $82.23 a barrel and Brent fell 2.37 per cent to $90.93 a barrel. Spot gold lost 2.86 per cent to $3,739.66 an ounce, silver fell 4.72 per cent to $45.16 an ounce, and copper declined 4.69 per cent to $12,606.00 a ton. US Treasury yields were slightly lower as oil prices dropped; the benchmark 10-year note fell 3.87 basis points to 5.064 per cent from 5.103 per cent late Tuesday, and the 30-year yield fell 4.49 basis points to 5.414 per cent from 5.459 per cent.
items.title: Global stocks slip on Nvidia results and a stronger dollar as Anthropic prepares to debut

items.summary: Nvidia reported record revenue for its fiscal third quarter, with profit and sales topping analysts' estimates according to CNBC. The company raised its full-year forecast through January 2028, now projecting revenue growth of 75% year over year. This was Nvidia's first earnings report since Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO; his departure followed an acknowledgment of a relationship with a businesswoman suspected of spying for China. Board Chair Harvey Jones told listeners at the start of the call that directors are not planning a return for Huang in the chief executive role, according to CNBC. In the broader market on Tuesday, the Dow fell more than 1% and the Nasdaq shed almost 1%, while the S&P 500 closed at its weakest point since July 29 and the Nasdaq hit an intraday low not seen since April, per CNBC. Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that the Federal Reserve would publish minutes from its October policy session at 2 p.m. ET; at that meeting policymakers held the federal funds rate target range steady at 3.75% to 4%, and Fed Governor Christopher Waller again pushed for raising rates by half a percentage point in December. CNBC also cited multiple sources indicating Anthropic is expected to price its IPO on Wednesday above the current range of $70 to $78 a share, while Quartz promoted its newsletter subscription.
items.title: Nvidia's post-Huang earnings report and mixed market reaction

items.summary: Mark Moerdler of Bernstein argued, per MarketWatch, that Oracle $ORCL shares are priced below value even in a severe downside scenario in which the company's AI data center operations disappear while the debt incurred for them remains. In that case he valued the stock at $133, above Tuesday's closing price of $115 and above its last close above $133 in late October. Moerdler described this as an extremely unlikely scenario short of a global 'AI Winter' in which generative AI fails within the next few years. He said investors may have already priced in a partial version of that risk, namely Oracle's inability to sublease or repurpose its existing leases, leaving it responsible for roughly $288 billion in data center lease obligations. Moerdler also contended that cloud-services demand could offset AI-related costs even if AI lost appeal, citing his forecast that the market might grow to as much as $1.4 trillion; he noted some of Oracle's data center leases run up to 19 years, which caps annual payments. He retained an outperform rating but warned investor sentiment may be slow to improve. Separately, Moerdler acknowledged many investors find Oracle's software business 'opaque' and that it could warrant a lower valuation. The article notes Oracle shares have fallen roughly 40% in 2026, heading for its weakest annual performance since 2001, as shareholders worry about returns and debt repayment from the data center buildout; CreditSights said earlier this month investors price Oracle's debt like high-yield despite an investment-grade rating. Oracle filed Nov. 2 to sell $10 billion of senior notes and $10 billion of common stock for its AI infrastructure, after shares fell more than 6% that day; the company carried $125.34 billion in debt on Aug. 31, mostly senior notes, and S&P Global Ratings cut it to BBB- in July, one step short of high-yield territory.
items.title: Bernstein: Oracle stock cheap even if AI data center business vanishes

items.summary: Reports by Semafor indicate Nvidia's board is split on whether to bring back former leader Jensen Huang as the company searches for a new chief executive. ARM and Marvell heads are reportedly among candidates considered to replace Huang. Further tensions may surface at an all-company town hall scheduled today. Separately, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos advised Nvidia to seek a successor internally rather than from outside; in his remarks at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World event, he argued that an external candidate would have a "vanishingly small chance of success" given the company's complex business.
items.title: Nvidia board divided over Jensen Huang's return as CEO

items.summary: Samsung launched the Galaxy S26 FE in India on 14 September for ₹79,999 (8 GB RAM, 256 GB storage). At launch it was priced only ₹8,000 below the Galaxy S26 (₹87,999) and roughly level with the iPhone 17. Two price increases later, however, the gap has widened: the S26 now costs ₹23,000 more than the FE, while the iPhone 17 is ₹19,901 more expensive. The first hike came on 28 September, when Samsung raised the Galaxy S26 (256 GB) from ₹87,999 to ₹1,02,999 — about a 17% increase that industry sources attributed to rising memory chip costs. Apple separately lifted the iPhone 17 (256 GB) from ₹82,900 to ₹99,900 following its September launch of the iPhone 18 Pro. The article notes that because the S26 FE launched before Samsung's 28 September price rise, readers should verify whether the FE's own price has changed since then and compare final prices after offers rather than listed prices; Samsung's launch offers include a cashback of up to ₹7,000 on bank cards or an exchange bonus of up to ₹8,000, but only one may be used. On specifications, the S26 FE carries a 6.7-inch AMOLED display at 120 Hz — described as the largest of the three phones — and Samsung's 3 nm Exynos 2500 processor; it has three rear cameras (a 50 MP main, a 12 MP ultra-wide, and an 8 MP telephoto with 3x optical zoom), a 4,900 mAh battery supporting 45 W wired and 15 W wireless charging, and Samsung's promise of up to seven generations of Android updates plus seven years of security updates. The Galaxy S26 has a smaller 6.3-inch 120 Hz screen with the newer Exynos 2600 chip; its three rear cameras include a 50 MP main, a 10 MP telephoto, and a 12 MP ultra-wide. items.summary: Fashion designer Karl Kani believes hip-hop needed its own clothing brand that reflected the music, culture, and style of the artists reshaping fashion in the 1990s. Speaking with NPR's A Martínez on Morning Edition, Kani said 'the marriage between Kani and hip-hop was, like, heaven-sent.' Born Carl Williams, he began designing clothes as a self-taught designer in Brooklyn, New York, in the late 1980s, inspired by watching his Haitian tailor father make matching linen suits for neighborhood sales. While hip-hop artists at the time wore Ralph Lauren, Tommy Hilfiger, and Calvin Klein—often favoring oversized fits, mixed colors, and their own looks rather than wearing them as intended—Kani recognized the appeal and helped turn that emerging streetwear style into a brand worn by Tupac Shakur, Aaliyah, and The Notorious B.I.G. Beyond dressing famous musicians, he aimed to build an international fashion business meant to endure past the decade that made it famous. His new memoir, Karl Kani: A Life By Design, reflects on the creative instincts and business decisions behind his brand's longevity. He explained that even his name—pronounced 'Can I?'—stemmed from doubts about building a clothing brand from the inner city; by calling himself Kani he forced himself to answer daily with 'Yes, I can.' After more than three decades in fashion, Kani also weighed in on skinny jeans, which he said many men wore poorly during that trend. His advice was to 'keep it simple, keep it slick and all black,' adding that you 'can never go wrong in all black.' The interview covered his memoir, the rise of his streetwear empire, hip-hop's influence on fashion, and why skinny jeans aren't for everyone, with a full version available via NPR's audio player. The item does not specify publication date or author beyond the interviewer A Martínez.
items.title: Karl Kani on dressing hip-hop royalty and his new memoir

E-commerce giant Amazon will invest $7 billion (€6.3bn) in renewable energy projects across India, buying some of the generated electricity to power operations such as data centres. The firm states these investments are part of a broader effort toward India's goal of 500 gigawatts of clean energy capacity by decade's end—a target the government estimates will require around $220 billion (€200bn) in investment overall. Amazon notes that coal and oil remain central to India's energy mix, with only 54 per cent of electricity currently coming from non-fossil fuel sources including solar, wind, and hydropower.

Kara Hurst, Amazon's chief sustainability officer, said the renewable investments reflect years of sustained effort across the industry. The company frames its emissions challenge partly through comparison: in 2022 it emitted 51.17 million metric tonnes of CO2e—more than Switzerland, Hong Kong, and Denmark combined—and by 2025 absolute carbon emissions rose 16 per cent, largely due to increased AI and data centre use; Google's emissions climbed 18 per cent while Microsoft's jumped 25 per cent in the same year.

To cut intensity, Amazon aims to reduce the carbon intensity of its electricity by 65 per cent by 2030 relative to a 2019 baseline—every unit consumed associated with 65 per cent fewer emissions—which supports its Climate Pledge goal of net-zero carbon by 2040. The Guardian reports that Amazon's transportation emissions have accelerated at an average of 18 per cent per year since the pledge began in 2019.

This new commitment builds on $4 billion (€3.3bn) already pledged, making Amazon one of India's leading corporate buyers of carbon-free electricity. Once operational, its contracted Indian projects will total more than 2 gigawatts—enough for over 3.5 million households' annual needs. The company describes itself as energy intensive due to packaging waste, shipping and logistics emissions, and the large volumes required by its global data centre network.

Amazon also announced four new utility-scale wind and solar projects totaling 934 megawatts: a 234 MW wind farm in Karnataka (its largest contracted Asian wind project), a 200 MW combined solar-wind site in Karnataka, a 300 MW solar project in Madhya Pradesh, and a 200 MW solar project in Rajasthan. All investments are to be made by 2030.

The article draws on an analysis published in the Journal Of Humanities and Social Science (2025) by Carolina Lisboa Sisnando regarding Amazon's energy intensity.
items.title: Amazon's €6.3bn India renewable energy pledge and its emissions context

items.summary: Zia Yusuf, Reform UK's home affairs spokesperson, told a Spectator magazine podcast that former Conservative defectors have been barred from shaping the party's immigration and border policy. He stated: "If you are in the category of being concerned about [former Conservatives being involved in Reform], none of the above are going to be involved in immigration policy or borders policy," adding that this effectively excludes most of the party's MPs, since he said Nigel Farage gave him the brief rather than them. Spectator editor and former Conservative minister Michael Gove challenged Yusuf over how Reform intended to reduce migration numbers given its large number of ex-Tory MPs, including Robert Jenrick, who had failed to do so while in government. Yusuf responded that "There's a reason why Nigel's given me this brief and not them." The comments follow a feud between Yusuf and Jenrick before the latter joined Reform earlier this year as economics spokesperson. Other former Conservative MPs among those defected include Suella Braverman, Danny Kruger, and Andrew Rosindell. Yusuf qualified his remarks by saying Braverman and Jenrick had either been sacked or resigned "over immigration policy or issues around culture." The claims raise questions about unity at the top of Reform, as both Braverman and Jenrick have engaged with immigration and cultural issues since joining, and Jenrick's June announcement of plans for a levy on migrant labour appears to contradict the assertion that former Tories play no role in immigration policy. Reform's grassroots members have long been suspicious of former Conservatives within the party; Farage has repeatedly pushed back against claims his party had become "the Conservative party 2.0" and said in January that Reform would not accept any more defectors after local elections on 7 May, yet Jenrick and others maintain strong influence. Tom Milford, a former spokesperson for Jenrick, now serves as Reform's head of press while continuing to produce social media videos covering topics including law and order. Yusuf and Richard Tice are often cited alongside Jenrick as the most likely successors to Farage should he stand down. Labour responded by saying Yusuf had "admitted that most Reform MPs can't be trusted on their migration policies." Anna Turley, Labour's minister of state for border security and asylum, said: "They don't trust two-thirds of their MPs to work on their immigration policies, yet they expect the country to trust them to secure Britain's borders."

The launch of a pro-Brexit campaign called Stay Out was one of the few genuine surprises this week in Westminster, even though its arguments drew on familiar playbook material. The video launched on X over the weekend and featured scenes of riots in France, champagne flowing in Brussels, and European politicians expressing desperation for Britain's cash. Among Westminster's anti-Brexit veterans there was immediate chatter about whether a counteroffensive was needed; one said the reaction was essentially "are they off to the races while we are still putting our pants on?" For now, rebuttals of Stay Out's claims — including that returning to the EU would cost £750m a week — are being handled mostly on social media by interested pro-rejoin freelancers without any central organisation. One MP said it is hard to launch a new pro-rejoin campaign until the direction of travel from the government is clear, noting existing groups like Best for Britain but arguing that making the case publicly would need a fresh movement and wanted to avoid the marches associated with People's Vote's blue berets.

Inside No 10 holds confidence that Andy Burnham can make his own case for a closer relationship with Europe without external pressure group support. Stay Out, run by former deputy chief Brexit negotiator Oliver Lewis, will be dubbed "the status quo campaign." Strategists point to Labour polling showing almost three-quarters — 71% — of all voters support a closer relationship with Europe if it helps bring down prices and grow the economy. They say Burnham can front any campaigning needed, arguing that Brexit has done more harm than good by damaging the economy, making travel harder for British people and businesses to trade, and fuelling the small boats crisis.

Some fear this mirrors David Cameron's 2016 attempt to make a remain case; however Labour strategists say it is fundamentally different. One said "Cameron could not make this kind of emotional connection with people, it was business leaders, facts and figures, and he was arguing for the status quo," adding that "We are the change campaign now." While some cabinet members urged caution last week over Burnham's uncertain direction on Europe — one noting they all easily lapse into worries about leave-voting seats — most trust the prime minister can set out a viable post-summit plan, with one saying Andy's way of doing things is laying out political argument.

Some close to Labour worry about leaving the argument solely to Burnham. One asked "Can they do this from the bowels of Downing Street?" and felt that rebuttal infrastructure — people ready to go out and fight and say it is bollocks — was not yet in place. Another remain campaign veteran expressed concern about being "left out on a limb," noting an apolitical maximalist pro-European campaign will emerge with willing helpers but nothing organised. Many who worked on the remain campaign and People's Vote are scarred by bitter infighting, particularly its final months; this is also true for some high-profile veterans of Vote Leave who want to steer clear of Stay Out. As in pro-Brexit campaigns there are often willing funders: one veteran said "It will happen because there will be money for it," but added they could not pay them any money to return to the issue.
items.title: Labour's response to Stay Out pro-Brexit campaign
